statement: Tom threads 14 beads in a row. The colours repeat: red, red, blue, red, red, blue, and so on. How many of the 14 beads are red?

choices.misconception: I counted the blue beads instead of the red ones.
I thought half of the beads are red, but each group of three has 2 red beads and only 1 blue.
I counted the 4 full groups of three and forgot the 2 beads at the end, which are both red.
I counted all the beads, the blue ones as well.

hints: Which part of the pattern repeats?
The part red, red, blue repeats. Write the 14 beads as R and B in groups of three, and watch out for any beads left over at the end.
Four groups of three use 12 beads, and each group has 2 red beads. Then 2 more beads are left. What colours are they?

solutions.reliable: The pattern repeats in groups of three: red, red, blue. Four groups use 12 beads, and with 2 red beads in each group they have 8 red beads. The 13th and 14th beads start a new group, so they are red and red. That makes 8 + 2 = 10 red beads. The idea to keep: find the part that repeats, then check the beads left over at the end.
solutions.elegant: Only every third bead is blue: the 3rd, 6th, 9th and 12th. That is 4 blue beads, so 14 take away 4 leaves 10 red beads. The idea to keep: sometimes it is quicker to count what is not asked about and take it away.

whyOnTest: Continuing a repeating pattern tests finding the part that repeats and not forgetting the leftover beads at the end.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
